description: Understanding AV blocks and conduction abnormalities
overview: This module covers atrioventricular blocks including first-degree, second-degree (Type I and Type II), and third-degree heart blocks, with focus on recognition and clinical implications.
objectives: Distinguish Type I from Type II second-degree AV block
Understand clinical implications of heart blocks

slides.title: First-Degree AV Block
slides.content: First-degree AV block: PR interval >0.20s, every P wave followed by QRS, benign condition, may be normal variant. Usually asymptomatic and requires no treatment.

slides.title: Second-Degree AV Block Type I
slides.content: Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach): progressive PR prolongation until P wave blocked, usually benign, located in AV node. QRS complexes are typically narrow.

quiz.question: What characterizes Mobitz Type I block?
quiz.explanation: Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach) is characterized by progressive PR interval prolongation until a P wave is blocked.

slides.title: Second-Degree AV Block Type II
slides.content: Mobitz Type II: fixed PR interval, sudden dropped QRS complexes, more serious than Type I, located below AV node, may progress to complete heart block.

quiz.question: What distinguishes Mobitz Type II from Type I?
quiz.explanation: Mobitz Type II has a fixed PR interval, unlike Type I which shows progressive prolongation.

slides.title: Third-Degree AV Block
slides.content: Complete heart block: no relationship between P waves and QRS complexes, ventricular escape rhythm, may require pacemaker. Atrial rate usually faster than ventricular rate.

quiz.question: What is the hallmark of third-degree AV block?
quiz.explanation: Third-degree AV block shows complete dissociation between atrial and ventricular activity.
